newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Debt markets close bid in NZ after soft GDP data.
newsitem.headline: Debt markets close bid in NZ after soft GDP data.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 93.12 (PREV 93.14) 90-DAYS 6.90 (PREV 6.92)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.55 PCT (PREV 6.55) US 5-YR 6.34 (PREV 6.36)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 773.10 (PREV 779.6)
New Zealand wholesale interest rates closed bid on Monday and were poised to fall further after soft GDP data endorsed the Reserve Bank's recent 100-point easing of monetary policy, dealers said.
A 0.5 percent fall in March quarter GDP was far weaker than expectations and showed that the economy actually contracted for the first quarter since September, 1992.

The soft number raised hopes of further easings in monetary conditions. But with conditions now stretched to the limit of the central bank's stated tolerance, much of the bullishness was priced into shorter-dated bonds rather than 90-day bank bills.
"I guess there's just a bit of caution in the 90-day area because that is the one variable that is identified in the Reserve Bank's published information," said a dealer.
At 773.85, the bank's Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) -- which measures the mix of 90-day rates and the exchange rate -- is already 1.15 points outside the comfort zone.
In its Monetary Policy Statement on Friday, the central bank said it wanted the MCI to average 825 in the September quarter but would tolerate a 50-point deviation either side of that level.

"The Reserve Bank's indentification (of conditions) is of course for the 90-day bills/currency trade-off. They don't look so closely at some of the mid-curve bonds -- the bond market has been pretty strong in that mid-curve area," noted the dealer.
"But those GDP numbers were quite a lot weaker than we were expecting, so that's nothing other than bullish for interest rate markets."
The 90-day rate, which initially rallied on the GDP release, quickly gave up most of its gains as the currency shed a quarter of a cent against the dollar. It closed two points lower at 6.90 percent.
Bonds, however, held their gains and most yields ended four to seven basis points lower on solid offshore and local demand.
"Bonds are in very, very good shape. The tone of the market is very good. It looks very bullish," said a senior bond dealer.
He said the long 11/06 bond had established a new range and could rally even deeper on Tuesday.

"I wouldn't even like guess at the potential of the 06s should they trade and close under 6.90 percent tomorrow. When a market makes a new low, there's no way of really knowing how far it's going to go. It could go five points but it could go 35."
-- Matthew Brockett, Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 473-3736
